item.title: Sri Lanka services exports rise 18.87-pct in October, driven by financial services
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Financial services grew 53.25 percent to 4.56 million dollars.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s services exports in October 2026 rose 18.87 percent to 360.21 million dollars, compared to the same period last year, the island’s Export Development Board said.

Financial services grew 53.25 percent to 4.56 million dollars.

Transport and logistics grew 24.72 percent to 197.87 million dollars.

Earnings from construction rose to 9.45 million dollars in October 2026, up 28.32 percent year-on-year.

Exports earnings from ICT/BPM rose 10.66 percent to 148.33 million dollars in October 2026 compared with October 2025.

Services exports reached an estimated 3,266.58 million dollars from January to October 2026, a year-on-year increase of 10.33 percent.

Sri Lanka goods exports rise 9.65-pct in October, boosted by spices, electronics

Total exports of goods and services for October 2026 was 15,281 million US dollars, up 6.03 percent from October 2025. (Colombo/Nov25/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka goods exports rise 9.65-pct in October, boosted by spices, electronics
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Apparel growth declined 3.82 percent year on year due to weak global demand.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s merchandise exports rose 9.65 percent to 1.26 billion dollars in October 2026 from a year ago, driven by electronic components, spices, and petro products, data from the export promotion office showed.

“Since September, the export sector has regained its usual momentum, and we expect growth exceeding 6.5 percent this year,” Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB) Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Mangala Wijesinghe said, citing Sri Lanka Customs data.

The electrical and electronic sector led growth over the 10 months by expanding close to 60 percent, alongside progress in rubber, food and beverages, spices, ICT, and logistics.

Spices and concentrates exports rose 76.90 percent.

Apparel growth declined 3.82 percent year on year due to weak global demand.

Tea exports continued to feel the impact of the conflict in West Asia, falling 6.22 percent.

Among key markets, exports to the United States crossed 2,500 million US dollars over the 10 months, while shipments to India, China, Belgium, Japan, Australia, Turkey, and Mexico grew sharply.

Total export revenue for the first 10 months from January to October crossed 15,281 million US dollars, a growth of 6 percent.

“A major focus is going beyond our traditional exports to develop innovative industries integrated with new technologies,” Wijesinghe said. (Colombo/Nov25/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka revises down 2026 export revenue target to US$18.5bn from US$20bn
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Exports have grown 6% in first 10 months of this year, less than expected 8%
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka will be able to achieve an export revenue of US$18.5 billion this year, 7.5 percent less than the Export Development Board’s (EDB) original target of US$20 billion, mainly due to sluggish foreign buying in tea and apparel, EDB Chairman and CEO Mangala Wijesinghe said.

The island nation has achieved an export growth of 6 percent to US$15.3 billion in both merchandise goods and services in the first 10 months of this year.

Originally, the government expected an ambitious US$20 billion in 2026 with an 8 percent growth.

EDB chief Wijesinghe said the initial target was US$20 billion and the country’s primary export sector is apparel, which accounts for more than 30% of total exports.

“Last year, in the growth we achieved surpassing 17 billion dollars, we saw a growth of over 6% from the apparel sector,” Wijesinghe told when asked if Sri Lanka still could achieve the US$20 billion target this year.

“Currently, due to the decrease in demand for the export sector in the international market, specifically due to the significant increase in costs and the drop in demand, there is a certain setback in the apparel sector,” he said.

“So, the setback in the apparel sector is what is affecting that decline. That is one aspect. The second factor is that there is currently a decrease of around 6% to 8% in our tea sector.”

“So overall, we had a target this year, and accordingly, we expect to achieve an export revenue growth exceeding 18.5 billion this year.”

Although exports recorded solid year-on-year growth in several months, achieving US$ 20 billion by year-end would require roughly US$ 4.72 billion across November and December alone, well above typical monthly export run-rates of around US$ 1.3 billion–US$ 1.7 billion.

The primary drag on meeting that headline ambition has been uneven performance in Sri Lanka’s two flagship traditional pillars, apparel and tea, amid softer external demand and geopolitical headwinds.

Apparel, which generates roughly US$ 5 billion annually and relies heavily on the United States market (around 40% of apparel exports), and tea, which depends significantly on Middle Eastern buyers (around 35% of tea exports), have both faced periods of contraction and demand softness during 2026.

While non-traditional and value-added segments such as coconut products, ICT/logistics services, and electrical components have provided pockets of resilience, they have not been large enough on their own to close the multi-billion-dollar gap left by sluggishness in apparel and tea.

Tight Fiscal, Monetary Stance

Fiscal consolidation under Sri Lanka’s reform program under the IMF has strengthened state revenue collections, but higher tax burdens and elevated input costs have squeezed export competitiveness in several ways, analysts say.

Broader tax coverage, stricter compliance, and elevated energy and utility costs have raised the cost of doing business for manufacturers and exporters.

Even where direct export sales are zero-rated or covered under specific schemes, exporters incur higher domestic costs on local suppliers, logistics, utilities, and services, compressing operating margins.

Higher corporate and income tax burdens, alongside high operating costs, have reduced retained earnings that exporters would otherwise deploy into automation, product upgrading, and new buyer acquisition.

When margins tighten, firms prioritize short-term cash preservation over long-term export diversification.

In competitive categories like apparel and tea, global retail buyers and importers frequently push back on price increases.

When domestic tax and cost pressures rise while global demand is cautious, exporters often have to absorb part of the cost squeeze themselves, blunting incentives to scale output aggressively.

Monetary policy has moved from supporting post-crisis recovery to leaning against renewed inflation pressures, with the Central Bank lifting the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) twice this year, creating distinct headwinds for exporters.

Exporters rely heavily on short-term working capital and trade credit to finance raw materials, fabric, tea leaf procurement, packaging, and shipping cycles before receiving buyer payments.

Higher policy rates and tighter bank liquidity push lending rates upward, increasing financing costs and making credit more selective, particularly for small and medium-sized exporters.

Tighter monetary conditions also raise the hurdle rate for borrowing to expand factory capacity, upgrade machinery, or adopt energy-saving equipment.

For export sectors trying to move up the value chain rather than compete solely on price, higher borrowing costs slow necessary productivity investments.

While tighter monetary policy and liquidity absorption help anchor inflation expectations and reinforce macro stability alongside Central Bank’s reserve accumulation, they also tighten domestic rupee liquidity.

For exporters whose costs are largely incurred in rupees while revenues are earned in foreign currency, a stable-to-firm rupee combined with higher domestic borrowing costs reduces windfall currency cushions and places greater weight on genuine productivity and cost efficiency. (Colombo/November 25/2026)

item.title: SriLankan Airlines adds fuel surcharge to break even by March after $35mn first-half loss
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: ECONOMYNEXT – SriLankan Airlines has added a small fuel surcharge to upcoming ticket sales in a bid to break even by March, after surging jet fuel prices pushed the national carrier to a 35 million US dollar loss in the first two quarters of the year, Deputy Minister of Ports and Civil Aviation Janitha Ruwan […]
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – SriLankan Airlines has added a small fuel surcharge to upcoming ticket sales in a bid to break even by March, after surging jet fuel prices pushed the national carrier to a 35 million US dollar loss in the first two quarters of the year, Deputy Minister of Ports and Civil Aviation Janitha Ruwan Kodithuwakku said.

Speaking on Derana’s Big Focus programme, Kodithuwakku said fuel accounts for 40 to 50 percent of an airline’s costs, and prices jumped from 2.10 dollars a gallon to between 4.40 and 4.50 dollars amid the situation in the Middle East.

Unlike many other countries that subsidized their national carriers, Sri Lankan Airlines did not take a fuel subsidy from the government and could not sharply raise ticket prices, he said.

“If by any chance that fuel price had stayed at 2.1 dollars per gallon, the airline would not have incurred this loss this year,” Kodithuwakku said.

To address the shortfall, the carrier introduced a separate fuel surcharge on upcoming ticket sales and aims to break even by the next season in March, noting that the airline still turned a profit in the first two months of this year.

Despite current fuel pressures, the airline has a strong revenue base with a 1-billion-dollar annual turnover—about one percent of gross domestic product and was comparable to a 23-aircraft operation.

Catering, ground handling, engineering, and cargo units all generate profits, while losses stem only from passenger operations where the airline faces competition, alongside past management issues, he said.

Last year, intervention by the former Chairman reduced overpriced aircraft lease rates from around 600,000 rupees a month to about 280,000 rupees, helping the carrier record a 4-million-dollar operational profit.

“We had signed aircraft lease agreements for huge prices that were not in the market. During last year, we resolved all of those,” Kodithuwakku said.

Management is now working to resolve costly engine service agreements, he added.

While the state must still pay off existing historical debts, the government aims to rebuild operations from zero so that, barring further global shocks, the airline no longer adds losses to the Treasury and taxpayers, Kodithuwakku said. (Colombo/Nov25/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka Cabinet approves purchasing of medicinal drugs from Indian, Chinese firms
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Bids were chosen after competitive bidding
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Cabinet of Ministers approved proposals to purchase medicinal drugs from India and China, the government said it its weekly Cabinet decision document.

The Cabinet approved the resolution to award the procurement to India-based M.J.Biopharm Private Limited to buy 2,700,000 Vials of Biphasic Isophane Insulin Injection (Human) BP 1,000 IU, 10 ml (30% Soluble, 70% Isophane) at a price of US$4.3 million for diabetic patients.

M.J.Biopharm was chosen out of two bids after its bid was found to be substantially responsive, the Cabinet document said.

The Cabinet also approved the purchase of 920,000 Pre-filled Syringes/Vials of Enoxaparin Sodium Injection 4,000 IU / 0.4 ml for the treatment of cardiac patients from lowest bidder, Chinese based Shenzhen Techdow Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd at US$828,000.

Shenzhen was chosen from seven (07) bids. (Colombo/November 25/2026)

item.title: Tourism destinations need more than visitors to deliver lasting benefit: ADB
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Governments should judge tourism development not only by how many people visit, but by what it delivers for local busine
item.content:encoded:
More visitors do not automatically mean better jobs or stronger local firms. Tourism destinations need coordinated investment, closer partnerships between government and businesses, and cooperation across borders to turn growth into lasting benefits.

Tourism destinations need more than rising visitor numbers to build stronger local economies. Governments must understand what businesses need and coordinate investments and reforms so that tourism creates jobs and benefits local communities.

That task has become more urgent as growth slows. International tourist arrivals in Asia and the Pacific increased by just 1% in the first half of 2026, down from 6% growth for the whole of 2025, according to UN Tourism. The Middle East conflict, the ongoing war in Ukraine, and a strengthening El Niño weighed on growth.

The slowdown exposed vulnerabilities in an important sector. Tourism accounts for nearly 10% of global gross domestic product (GDP), and creates jobs and business opportunities, including for women and young people. Well-managed tourism can also help protect cultural heritage and nature.

Tourism projects need a clear understanding of the market: who is likely to visit, how much they may spend, and which policies and regulations help or hinder businesses. Reliable data and regular dialogue with the private sector can help governments identify opportunities and barriers to investment.

From April to September 2026, Southeast Asian tourism ministries brought businesses together to discuss opportunities and what was holding back investment. The meetings revealed differences between government ambitions and business decisions. Some ministries wanted new air routes to bring more visitors, but airlines said they needed better data on demand before committing to add flights.

Better market information and regular dialogue can help governments identify what is holding a destination back. Governments can then target policy reforms, build stronger institutions, invest in the right infrastructure, and support risk-sharing measures that are most likely to encourage private investment. Businesses, in turn, gain a clearer understanding of government priorities and plans.

Invest in what destinations need

Understanding the market is only a start. A destination also needs transport, reliable water and electricity, effective public institutions, and businesses able to meet visitors’ needs and expectations. These need to work together if tourism is to benefit residents.

A changing climate, environmental degradation, overcrowding, and poorly managed development can damage the natural and cultural assets that attract visitors. Protecting those assets is an investment in a destination’s competitiveness and its ability to withstand sudden changes or crises.

Good plans bring these needs together and clarify who is responsible for meeting them. They coordinate the timing of transport links, utilities, changes to visa and business rules, and efforts to attract investment. The aim is not simply to bring in more tourists, but to protect heritage and nature, strengthen local businesses, widen opportunities, and keep more of the benefits within communities.

Sri Lanka is rebuilding its tourism industry after setbacks including the coronavirus pandemic and a 2022 economic crisis. Infrastructure investment and targeted policy reforms aligned with its 10-year national tourism policy aim to turn recovering demand into private investment, more competitive businesses, and jobs.

Work across borders to strengthen tourism

Planning also needs to look beyond national borders. Destinations share challenges related to air connections, geopolitical uncertainty, and changing travel patterns. Working together can help countries align policies, coordinate investment, and make cross-border journeys easier.

The Almaty–Bishkek Economic Corridor shows how regional cooperation can support tourism. Linking Almaty in Kazakhstan with Bishkek in the Kyrgyz Republic, the corridor already hosts an estimated 8.4 million tourists a year. Its updated master plan identifies $900 million in priority investments across the two countries, including an Almaty air hub and faster land connections to Lake Issyk-Kul in the Kyrgyz Republic, the second-largest high-mountain lake in the world.

The countries are also coordinating the rebuilding of border crossings to make travel easier. Their shared approach allows them to develop and protect natural and cultural attractions on both sides of the border.

Governments should judge tourism development not only by how many people visit, but by what it delivers for local businesses and communities. That means using market evidence and working with businesses to identify barriers, then coordinating reforms and investments within countries and across borders.

Countries cannot control global travel demand, but they can strengthen destinations’ ability to withstand shocks and keep more of tourism’s benefits in local communities.

item.title: Sri Lanka to start partial operations at East Container Terminal
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: The state-run Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) awaits pending straddle carriers
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka will start partial operations at the Colombo Port’s East Container Terminal (ECT) by the end of this month after completing testing, Deputy Minister of Ports and Civil Aviation Janitha Ruwan Kodithuwakku said.

The terminal will initially run at minimum capacity while the state-run Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) awaits pending straddle carriers. Kodithuwakku said the first 15 straddle carriers are expected to arrive around September next year, when the infrastructure required for 50 percent capacity will be built.

Procurement for the next 15 carriers is expected to finish within the following four months, with infrastructure for 100 percent capacity set to be completed by the first quarter of 2028. Officials will run a parallel marketing plan so the terminal can reach full capacity around mid-2028.

ECT construction began in 2022 and was originally set to finish in 2024, when only 10 percent was completed, Kodithuwakku told TV Derana’s “Big Focus” program. Following government intervention, about 60 percent more work was finished, bringing overall progress to 90 percent in 2026.

To avoid traditional state-sector delays, the government is forming a new company 100 percent owned by the SLPA to run the terminal with private-sector efficiency, while discussions continue on future private involvement.

“There is no decision yet on sharing ownership, as we want a model that competes with other terminals and brings maximum returns to the Ports Authority,” Kodithuwakku said.

The SLPA has already funded the entire ECT investment, so no new capital is needed. Instead, the terminal needs strong marketing because 85 percent of Colombo’s cargo is transshipment business controlled by about 10 major global shipping lines.

Addressing 2020 trade union protests against a private partnership—including by unions linked to the National People’s Power(NPP)—Kodithuwakku said they opposed old shareholding deals meant to cover up state inefficiency, and kept ECT under the SLPA as promised.

“Right now, we do not need an investment for the East Container Terminal because the Ports Authority has finished investing, but we need a marketing strategy,” he said.

The SLPA will operate the terminal initially while officials assess whether full state operation or a more advanced model brings the greatest benefit to the country and the Ports Authority. (Colombo/Nov25/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s reserve ratio hike to lock up Rs140bn, cost banks Rs12bn in interest: First Capital
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: "The higher reserve ratio imposes a cost on banks, but it offers gains in inflation control and stability,"
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s central bank decision to raise the Statutory Reserve Ratio (SRR) for the first time in more than three years will permanently lock up about 140 billion rupees of commercial bank cash and cost lenders roughly 12 billion rupees a year in lost interest income, First Capital Research said in its latest research flash note.

At its November 2026 monetary policy review, the Central Bank raised the SRR—the share of customer rupee deposits that banks must hold with the regulator without earning interest—by 100 basis points, or one percentage point, from 2 percent to 3 percent, effective December 9, 2026.

The move came alongside a 25 basis point increase in the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) and marks the first change to the reserve ratio since August 2023, when it was cut from 4 percent to 2 percent, and the first hike since September 2021.

First Capital said the decision ends the low reserve ratio policy maintained since 2023 and reflects a stronger push to mop up spare cash in the banking system.

Excess liquidity—the leftover cash banks hold after meeting minimum reserve requirements—has climbed sharply in recent months to record highs of more than 475 billion rupees, largely generated by the Central Bank buying US dollars from the market.

“The higher reserve ratio imposes a cost on banks, but it offers gains in inflation control and stability,” First Capital Research said in a flash note.

Rupee deposits subject to the reserve requirement stood at about 13.7 trillion rupees at the end of August 2026, meaning the extra one percentage point will absorb around 140 billion rupees into non-interest-bearing Central Bank accounts.

Based on the Standing Deposit Facility Rate of 8.50 percent—set 50 basis points below the OPR—First Capital estimates this will result in roughly 12 billion rupees a year in foregone pre-tax interest income across the banking sector.

In return, the Central Bank gains a permanent tool to absorb surplus cash created by its foreign exchange purchases, keep market interest rates aligned with its policy rate, and support a planned slowdown in credit growth.

A tighter reserve framework had been on the cards since the Central Bank’s 2026 Policy Agenda earlier this year, especially as Sri Lanka’s 2 percent ratio was low compared to regional peers such as India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Indonesia.

Before raising the ratio, the Central Bank removed a rule at the end of September 2026 that allowed banks to count cash held in their vaults toward reserve requirements.

Since mid-2026, the regulator had also been absorbing cash temporarily through open market repo operations at two to three times the level of overnight liquidity, pointing to the need for a more permanent fix.

“Indirectly, this can also be a signal of the Central Bank’s intention to purchase more and more dollars from the market going forward,” First Capital analysts said.

Once the 140 billion rupees is absorbed, excess liquidity in the market is expected to decline toward 200 billion to 300 billion rupees by the end of 2026.

However, First Capital noted that overall liquidity will remain elevated for some time, as the reserve ratio increase absorbs only part of the surplus cash in the banking system. (Colombo/Nov25/2026)

item.title: Foreign YouTuber slams ‘failed management’ at Sri Lanka’s Sigiriya over two-hour queues
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: "This is nothing but failed management of an object. I mean, you charge 35 USD for entrance,” he said.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Heavy crowding and two-hour queues to get to the top at Sri Lanka’s Sigiriya Rock Fortress have drawn criticism from a foreign travel YouTuber, who urged tourism authorities to introduce hourly tickets to manage visitor flow better.

In a video documenting his visit, YouTuber “Roman_onboard” described long delays and heavy crowding forced him and his partner to leave the ascend half-way, noting that foreign visitors faced long waits despite paying a 35 US dollar entrance fee.

“I would say from my point of view this is nothing but failed management of an object. I mean, you charge 35 USD for entrance,” he said.

While praising the site’s beauty and history as worth the trip, he warned that travelers pressed for time could miss out and urged the Sri Lanka Ministry of Tourism to fix the issue.

“I hope that Sri Lanka Ministry of Tourism will fix somehow this problem. You just need to sell tickets by hour, for a specific time frame,” he said.

Sigiriya, managed by the Central Cultural Fund (CCF), remains Sri Lanka’s most-visited cultural heritage site. Official Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA) data shows the rock and museum drew 1,086,918 visitors in 2025, comprising 582,687 foreign tourists and 504,231 domestic visitors. Foreign visitors to Sigiriya accounted for roughly 24.7 percent of all international arrivals to the island last year.

Monthly visitor counts for Sigiriya in 2026 are not publicly released, as the SLTDA publishes site-specific figures once a year. However, CCF Director General Nilan Cooray noted in May 2026 that the site averages around 2,500 foreign visitors daily. (Colombo/Nov25/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka stocks trend up 0.56-pct, driven by LOLC, DCSL
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Positive contributors to the ASPI were PGP Glass, Distilleries Company, LOLC Holdings, Access Engineering
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Colombo Stock Exchange opened higher on Wednesday, CSE data showed, with the benchmark All Share Price Index moving up 0.56 percent.

The ASPI was up 119.73 points at 21,362.25, while the more liquid S&P SL20 was up 0.68 percent, or 41.04 points, at 6,087.21.

Positive contributors to the ASPI were PGP Glass Ceylon (up 6.56 percent at 61.70 rupees), Distilleries Company of Sri Lanka (up 1.21 percent at 58.70 rupees), LOLC Holdings (up 1.93 percent at 409.75 rupees), Access Engineering (up 2.93 percent at 84.40 rupees), and Asiri Hospital Holdings (up 6.90 percent at 31 rupees).

Overseas Realty (Ceylon) (down 1.54 percent at 51.20 rupees), Odel (down 2.29 percent at 12.80 rupees), Colombo Fort Investments (down 3.15 percent at 300 rupees), and First Capital Treasuries (down 0.75 percent at 26.40 rupees) were top negative contributors.

Market turnover was 239.46 million rupees. The Transportation sector led turnover with 34.47 million rupees. (Colombo/Nov25/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka defends tourism revenue math, rupee gains amid opposition criticism
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: "You introduced this formula retrospectively to inflate and show a higher figure for declining tourism revenue,” Rajapak
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s government defended its tourism earnings figures in parliament on Tuesday, rejecting opposition claims that officials changed the calculation formula to hide falling dollar income.

Opposition lawmaker Namal Rajapaksa questioned why the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority revised its monthly revenue formula in May 2026 and applied it back to January.

“Today there is a question in society whether you introduced this formula retrospectively to inflate and show a higher figure for declining tourism revenue,” Rajapaksa told parliament.

In May 2026, the tourism authority updated its calculation method using country-specific arrival data, average stay, and daily spending. The revision raised estimated earnings for January through April, after earlier data showed sharp drops in March and April following the U.S. and Israel bombing of Iran from February 28.

Tourism Minister Vijitha Herath said revenue has not fallen, explaining that the new calculation follows a globally accepted United Nations tourism methodology with a different sample size. Under the updated calculation, estimated daily spending per visitor changed from 182 dollars to 143 dollars.

“It is according to that calculation that a decrease in revenue is shown, not because of the arrival of so-called budget tourists,” Herath said.

Herath said India is Sri Lanka’s top tourist market, followed by the United Kingdom, with six European nations including Germany in the top ten.

Deputy Tourism Minister Ruwan Ranasinghe said over 3,000 flights were cancelled due to wars in the Middle East and between Russia and Ukraine. He added that earnings in rupee terms rose from 712 billion rupees in 2018 to 967 billion rupees in 2025, while Tourism Development Levy collections doubled from two billion to four billion rupees. (Colombo/Nov24/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka faces 419-engineer shortfall in state service amid allowance row
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Only 1,153 officers were in service as of November 18, 2026, Public Administration Minister A. H. M. H. Abayarathna said
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s state engineering service faces an acute shortage of 419 engineers out of an approved cadre of 1,572, as union action over allowances and years of departures weigh on public projects, Parliament heard.

Only 1,153 officers were in service as of November 18, 2026, Public Administration Minister A. H. M. H. Abayarathna said in response to Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa.

The sharpest gap is at entry level, where 355 of 1,143 Grade III posts are vacant, leaving 285 Grade I and II officers covering Grade III duties, alongside 51 Grade I and 13 Special Grade vacancies.

The crisis coincides with a work-to-rule and sick-leave campaign by state engineers demanding a separate specialized allowance, known as the FACT allowance.

“Due to the engineering sector implementing a work-to-rule campaign and a sick-leave campaign, this situation severely affects the implementation of your own budget proposals,” Premadasa said.

Premadasa urged a new circular granting a separate 75,000-rupee allowance to curb brain drain. The dispute stems from a June 2024 circular replacing a 15,000-rupee allowance with a 25,000-rupee one, while a July 2024 Cabinet decision went unimplemented due to an election period.

Abayarathna said no extra funds were allocated in the budget and warned against piecemeal changes before a broader pay review.

“Providing an allowance while disparities exist could further widen that disparity,” Abayarathna told parliament.

He said a Salaries and Pensions Commission chaired by Ashoka Peiris will submit an interim report in January. Basic salaries for all-island services are already rising 72.53 percent to 82,150 rupees by January 2027, with allowance revisions planned for 2028.

Between 2021 and 2025, 328 engineers left and 68 went abroad on long-term leave. After a 2023–2024 hiring freeze, 200 were recruited in 2025, and applications were called in November 2026 for 201 open and 66 limited posts, alongside plans to replace 25-year-old vehicles.

Premadasa faulted the government’s two-year record and cited remarks of an overflowing Treasury, while Abayarathna blamed the opposition for past brain drain.

“Even though there is money in the State Treasury as the Leader of the Opposition says, as a government, we have the need to identify such limitations and act accordingly,” he said. (Colombo/Nov24/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s Bank of Ceylon to list 13-pct debentures
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: five-year debenture will offer a fixed coupon of 12.75 percent per annum, seven-year debenture will carry a fixed coupon
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s state-owned Bank of Ceylon (BOC) will list a Basel III-compliant debenture issue with a non-viability write-down feature on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) on November 25, according to a market filing.

The issue consists of two listed debt securities carrying fixed annual coupon rates.

A five-year debenture will offer a fixed coupon of 12.75 percent per annum, payable annually, while a seven-year debenture will carry a fixed coupon of 13.00 percent per annum, also payable on an annual basis.

The securities would commence trading following their listing on November 25.

Bank of Ceylon is Sri Lanka’s largest state-owned commercial bank. (Colombo/Nov25/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s national inflation rises to 41-month high of 8.5-pct in October; transport leads
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Increase in transport prices result in non-food inflation to rise
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s nation-wide inflation index, as measured by the National Consumer Price Index (NCPI) on a year-on-year basis, rose to 8.5 percent in October 2026, up from 8.1 percent a month ago, data from the state statistics office showed.

It stood at its highest since June 2023, official data showed.

The NCPI, an alternative to the widely watched Colombo Consumer Price Index, rose 0.4 percent, in October 2026, registering 225.1 compared to 224.2 in September 2026.

The year-on-year inflation of the food group increased to 7.2 percent in the last month from 6.9 percent in September 2026.

Year-on-year inflation for the non-food group accelerated to 9.5 percent from 9.1 percent a month ago, mainly driven by transport cost after the government raised fuel prices in the end of October.

The NCPI includes 485 items representing consumption of Sri Lanka households. It is compiled three weeks after the end of each month and the release of the key index Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI). (Colombo/October 21/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka rupee closes at 332.55/60 to US dollar spot, bond yields rise

item.content:encoded:

item.title: Foreign outflows from Sri Lanka rupee bonds continue for fifth straight week
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Sri Lanka has suffered Rs. 42.5 billion worth foreign outflows from the rupee bonds in last seven weeks.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Foreign investors sold Sri Lanka rupee bonds and exited the island nation’s risk-free assets for a fifth straight week in the week ended on November 18, Central Bank data showed, amid depreciation in the rupee currency.

With the latest outflows, the island nation has seen net foreign selling in seven out of the last 22 weeks.

Offshore investors sold a net Rs. 8,583 million (US$26 million) worth of Sri Lanka rupee bonds in the week ended on November 19.

The net selling extended the net foreign outflows from the rupee bonds to Rs. 42.5 billion in the last seven weeks.

Despite outflows in the last five weeks, the island nation has seen a total inflow of around Rs. 29.6 billion into local currency bonds this year through Nov 19, following a net inflow of 71.5 billion rupees last year.

The latest foreign selling comes after the U.S. mid-term election showed strong checks and balances for Trump’s presidential powers and hopes of an end to hostilities against Iran. It also came as the Israel Prime Minister failed to secure a majority in his election.

The rupee had been steady for more than three years before the sharp depreciation in May with the Central Bank citing higher oil and vehicle imports amid a lingering conflict in the Middle East.

The rupee has fallen 6.9 percent through November 13, this year.

Globally, investors are cautious about economic growth due to the impact of the latest Middle East escalation.

The rupee has stabilized after the Central Bank raised its key monetary policy rate by 100 basis points in May to curb inflationary pressure stemming from higher demand. The Central Bank, siting higher inflationary expectation raised the policy rate by 25 basis points on Friday (20).

The island nation has seen an uptick in inflation in the last seven months following a nearly 50 percent hike in fuel prices.

The government raised fuel prices in the last week of October, raising further inflationary concerns.

Before the May rate hike, the Central Bank kept its key policy rates steady since May 2025 after reducing them by 825 basis points over 24 months since June 2023 and foreign investors have been buying rupee bonds. (Colombo/November 23/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka stocks close down 0.60-pct, turnover Rs1.05bn
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Positive contributors to the ASPI were Digital Mobility, Ambeon Holdings, Hatton National Bank, and Janashakthi
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Colombo Stock Exchange closed down on Monday, CSE data showed, with the benchmark All Share Price Index moving down 0.60 percent.

The ASPI was down 127.20 points at 21,242.52, while the more liquid S&P SL20 was down 0.34 percent, or 20.52 points, at 6,054.76.

Positive contributors to the ASPI were Digital Mobility Solutions Lanka (up 5.11 percent at 185 rupees), Ambeon Holdings (up 2.99 percent at 34.50 rupees), Singer (Sri Lanka) (up 1.08 percent at 74.90 rupees), Hatton National Bank (up 0.19 percent at 394.50 rupees), and Janashakthi Insurance (up 3.17 percent at 39.10 rupees).

Dialog Axiata (down 1.04 percent at 47.50 rupees), Carson Cumberbatch (down 2.05 percent at 680 rupees), Hayleys (down 0.98 percent at 228 rupees), Commercial Bank of Ceylon (down 0.23 percent at 213.50 rupees), and Dilmah Ceylon Tea Company (down 10.39 percent at 1,407.75 rupees) were top negative contributors.

Market turnover was 1.05 billion rupees. Food, beverage and tobacco led turnover with 248.25 million rupees. (Colombo/Nov23/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka opens draft labour law reforms for public views, briefs lawmakers
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Allowing members of the public and relevant stakeholders to submit their views and proposals.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka has published the first four chapters of a proposed Labour Standards Bill online to gather public feedback as officials move to review and combine the country’s labour laws.

The drafted chapters are now available on the Ministry of Labour’s official website, labourmin.gov.lk, allowing members of the public and relevant stakeholders to submit their views and proposals.

Ministry of Labour officials briefed Members of Parliament on the planned reforms during a special meeting held at Parliament on November 18.

The session was chaired by Minister Anil Jayantha, Chairman of the Ministerial Consultative Committee on Labour Affairs.

An expert committee appointed with Cabinet approval is formulating the new legal framework to update Sri Lanka’s labour rules for the current and future world of work.

Officials told lawmakers that the main goal is to review existing major labour laws and bring them into one updated framework.

The proposed reforms are being developed under four main areas: labour standards, occupational health and safety, industrial relations and disputes, and trade union rights.

Under the new framework, authorities plan to cover paternity leave, maternity protection, and the prevention of violence and harassment in the workplace.

The proposed provisions also address working hours, leave, overtime, making employment contracts formal, and ensuring a safe working environment.

In addition, the laws will cover social security benefits and the rights of part-time employees.

Ministry officials said views from relevant stakeholders—including trade unions, employers, and employee representatives—are expected to be taken into account while shaping the proposed laws.

Deputy Minister of Labour Mahinda Jayasinghe, Members of Parliament, and a group of officials from the Ministry of Labour also attended the meeting. (Colombo/Nov23/2026)
